**Friday's seminar, second hour** · Today we meet a community of people inventing a language from nothing: making up words for shapes that have never had names, and we ask a simple question: does the *size* of a community shape the language it builds? Everything runs in RStudio on UCloud; use your Methods01 setup to get started.
:::

## The question

Every human language was invented by a community. The words of English are shaped over many generations by people using them with one another. In the lecture, we explored processes of **cultural evolution**: structure that emerges from use. And these processes raise a question we can actually test. If communities build languages, do the properties of the community leave their fingerprint on the language itself?

Raviv, Meyer and Lev-Ari (2019) brought that question into the laboratory. They gathered communities of volunteers and handed each one a private world to name: a set of novel shapes with no existing words. On every turn, one member saw a shape and typed a made-up word for it; the others chose, from an array, the shape they thought the word meant. Everyone saw whether the guess landed, then they swapped roles, and played again for fourteen rounds in all. Round by round, the invented words drifted from a scramble of private guesses toward a vocabulary the whole community came to share.

The design had two main conditions. Some communities had four members; others had eight. That is the only knob the experimenters touched, and the question for today is whether it changed the properties of the languages that grew.

Place a bet before you go on. A community of four is intimate: few people, little to track, easy to fall into step. A community of eight is busier: more partners, more words in play, more to coordinate.

**Which community do you think ends up communicating *more accurately* by the final round: the group of four or eight?** Write your guess down and explain why you have chosen it. You will settle this question with the data, in Exercise 1.

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of this seminar, you will be able to:

- Read raw experimental data and watch a shared word emerge from many competing ones.
- Measure whether communication improves over time, and compare small communities with large ones.
- Discover, in the words themselves, that the languages become *structured*.
- Explain, using the data, how the size of a community shapes the language it builds.

## How it works

Same format as the last two weeks. Work with a partner. Short pages that show you something, then pages where **you write the code**: wherever you see `____`, that's yours. Every function is one you have already used; nothing new today, the tools just travel to a new place.

Start with [Block 1 · Meet the data](01_meet_the_data.qmd).
